As part of the ongoing effort to ensure appropriate sanitary living conditions for civilians across the Gaza Strip, COGAT reached out directly to Gazan residents through its Arabic-language social media page and asked them to report locations where waste removal was urgently needed, as we have done with water distribution. Following the many responses received from the civilian population, COGAT reviewed the requests and coordinated with local and international partners to operate waste removal services in many areas across the Gaza Strip. Specifically, after many civilian reports from the area, waste was removed from Al-Nadim Street, the Al-Zeitoun neighborhood, the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, and from the A. Dahra area to the Jasser building in Khan Yunis. The waste removals at these locations were not a one-time operation. International organizations and local authorities will continue to operate there on an ongoing basis to clear the waste and deal with health hazards. Projects such as this waste-removal operation and last month’s water supply project prove how this direct channel of communication helps identify specific needs on the ground and enables a faster and more focused humanitarian response.

Today, 130 Gazan patients and their escorts left through the Kerem Shalom crossing in a coordinated medical evacuation. Through Jordan, these patients will fly to a third country to receive medical treatment, coordinated by COGAT in full cooperation with the UN and the international community. In addition, the Rafah Border Crossing has remained operational. To date, roughly 5,500 people have entered, and 5,800 have exited Gaza via the border crossing since the start of the ceasfire. Israel remains committed to coordinating the appropriate medical response for the Gazan civilian population, and will continue coordinating medical evacuations together with the @WHO.

A few days ago, @UNICEF published a report determining that acute malnutrition rates in Gaza are as low as 0.2%–0.8%. The report notes that this rate reflects greater stability than in many other countries in the region. These findings align with the humanitarian report that we in COGAT published several weeks ago, which determined that the volume of food entering the Gaza Strip during the ceasefire significantly exceeded humanitarian needs. Since the start of the ceasefire, over 2 million tons of food have entered Gaza. This massive influx has led to: 📉 A sharp drop in food prices. 🥗 Greater dietary diversity in local markets. 🍞 Dozens of active bakeries and community kitchens. COGAT’s coordination efforts, in cooperation with the international community, have maintained a stable food situation in Gaza. The data speaks for itself. Backed by hard facts, it is clear that the steady flow of aid is meeting and exceeding humanitarian needs, securing long-term stability on the ground. Read COGAT’s full report here: https://bit.ly/4p8iCOp
